issues.legal_issue: Criminal proceedings should be quashed where the record, viewed as a whole, shows no criminal intent or act and continuation of the prosecution would amount to an abuse of process.
material_facts: The association obtained leased land to build a cricket stadium, with nominal rent for the stadium land approved under the applicable lease rules for a public purpose.
Additional land for a club house and hotel was leased for commercial use at commercial rates in accordance with the applicable rules.

Senior government officials examined and approved the land arrangements, but the officials who played significant roles in the decisions were not prosecuted or did not receive prosecution sanction; some more junior officials remained accused.
The association’s conversion to a not-for-profit company followed the cricket board’s mandate, and the State retained ownership of the leased land while the facilities were used by the public.
The proceedings alleged criminal conduct in the land arrangements and related acts, but the Court found that the record did not disclose criminal intent or acts constituting an offence.
issues.conclusion: The Court set aside the High Court’s refusal to quash the proceedings and quashed both FIRs, holding that no criminal case was made out and that continuation of the proceedings would serve no purpose.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, inherent power is exercised sparingly and cautiously to prevent abuse of process or secure the ends of justice, including where accepted allegations do not prima facie constitute an offence or the proceeding is clearly abusive. The Court applied State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal, Indian Oil Corporation v. NEPC India Ltd., Vineet Kumar v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and State of Karnataka v. M. Devendrappa. It also considered that the nominal rent for the stadium was authorized under the proviso to Rule 8(1) of the Himachal Pradesh Lease Rules, 1993, and that the association’s conversion was under Section 25 of the Companies Act, 1956.

issues.definition: When a criminal proceeding is being reviewed and the land arrangements, official decision-making, organizational conversion, and continuing public ownership and use have the stated characteristics, the proceedings are quashed.

issues.legal_issue: Filing a chargesheet and taking cognizance while a challenge to the refusal to quash an FIR is pending does not make that challenge infructuous, and a related writ challenging the resulting proceedings may be entertained in the same procedural circumstances.
material_facts: The challenge to the refusal to quash the FIRs was pending when the investigation was completed and chargesheets were filed.
A related writ petition challenging the chargesheets was filed while the appeals concerning the refusal to quash the FIRs were pending.
The Court considered the challenges together and held that the appeals had not become infructuous; it entertained the writ petition in view of those particular circumstances.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the argument that the appeals had become infructuous and entertained the related writ petition; after quashing the FIRs, it held that the cognizance order stood vitiated.
issues.legal_principle: The Court dealt with the issue on the particular procedural facts: the challenge to the refusal to quash was already pending when the chargesheets and cognizance order followed, and the related writ was brought in that setting. It entertained the writ in those circumstances and stated that quashing the FIRs vitiated the cognizance order. No earlier case was identified by the Court as the basis for this procedural ruling.

predicates.related_writ_challenged_resulting_procee: A related writ petition challenged the proceedings that followed the investigation.

issues.definition: When a challenge to refusal to quash remains pending as a chargesheet and cognizance follow, and a related writ challenges those proceedings, the pending challenge remains justiciable and the related writ may be entertained.
